title: 03 — Trees, Boosting and Tuning
html:
03 — Trees, Boosting and Tuning

The one idea: a decision tree asks a sequence of yes or no questions about the features. Gradient boosting adds many small trees, each one correcting the errors left by the ones before. On tabular data (most financial data) it is usually the strongest baseline you can build.

1. What it is

Model Idea Strengths Weaknesses
Decision tree Split the data on the feature and threshold that most reduce error, then repeat Readable, captures interactions, no scaling needed Overfits when deep, unstable
Random forest Many deep trees on bootstrap samples, averaged Robust, few settings Large, less accurate than boosting on many tasks
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) Shallow trees added one by one, each fitting the current residuals, scaled by a learning rate State of the art on tabular data, handles missing values More settings, can overfit, needs early stopping

2. Why it matters

  • Credit scores, fund-flow predictions, anomaly scores and matching models are mostly tabular, and boosted trees win there more often than neural networks.
  • Tuning (choosing depth, learning rate, number of trees) decides whether the model generalises or memorises.
  • Explaining tree models (feature importance, SHAP values) is expected in regulated finance.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: one split

A stump is a tree with one split. To find it, try each feature and candidate threshold, predict the mean on each side, and keep the split with the smallest squared error. A full tree repeats this inside each side until a depth or minimum size is reached.

3.2 Intermediate: boosting

---
title: Gradient boosting — each tree fits what is still wrong
---
flowchart LR
    B["Start: predict the mean"] --> R1["Residuals<br/>(actual − prediction)"]
    R1 --> T1["Fit small tree 1"]
    T1 --> U1["prediction += lr × tree 1"]
    U1 --> R2["New residuals"]
    R2 --> T2["Fit small tree 2"]
    T2 --> U2["prediction += lr × tree 2"]
    U2 --> MORE["... repeat N rounds,<br/>stop when validation stops improving"]
  • For squared error, residuals are exactly the negative gradient. Other losses (log-loss) use their own gradients, which is why it is called gradient boosting.
  • A small learning rate with more trees generalises better. Stop with early stopping on validation loss.

3.3 Senior: settings that matter, and tuning

Setting (XGBoost / LightGBM names) Effect
learning_rate / eta Step size per tree. Smaller is safer and needs more trees
n_estimators plus early stopping Number of trees, chosen by validation
max_depth / num_leaves Interaction complexity
min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf Stops tiny, noisy leaves
subsample, colsample_bytree Randomness that reduces overfitting
reg_lambda, reg_alpha L2 and L1 penalties on leaf weights
scale_pos_weight / is_unbalance Class imbalance

Tuning on Databricks (checked 2026-10-26): Hyperopt is no longer maintained, and is not pre-installed from Databricks Runtime ML 17.0. Databricks recommends Optuna for single-node tuning, and Ray Tune for distributed tuning.

# Not run: requires optuna and lightgbm.
import optuna, lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

def objective(trial):
    params = {"learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 0.01, 0.3, log=True),
              "num_leaves": trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 8, 128, log=True),
              "min_data_in_leaf": trial.suggest_int("min_data_in_leaf", 20, 400, log=True),
              "feature_fraction": trial.suggest_float("feature_fraction", 0.5, 1.0),
              "objective": "binary", "verbose": -1}
    model = lgb.train(params, lgb.Dataset(X_train, y_train), num_boost_round=2000,
                      valid_sets=[lgb.Dataset(X_valid, y_valid)],
                      callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)])
    return roc_auc_score(y_valid, model.predict(X_valid))

study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize")
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50)
print(study.best_params)

Explaining: use SHAP values (the shap package) for per-prediction contributions. Built-in "gain" importance is biased towards high-cardinality features.

4. Working code

The script implements a stump and gradient boosting from scratch on made-up fund-flow data, then tunes the number of rounds and the learning rate on a validation split, and reports the winner on test. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
# Made-up regression: a fund's next-month flow (% of AUM) depends non-linearly on past return and size.
n = 1500
past_ret = rng.normal(0, 4, n)                 # last 3-month return, %
log_aum = rng.normal(7, 1.2, n)                # log of AUM in crore
y = np.where(past_ret > 2, 1.5, -0.5) + 0.3 * np.tanh(past_ret / 3) - 0.4 * (log_aum > 8) + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)
X = np.column_stack([past_ret, log_aum])
tr, va, te = np.split(rng.permutation(n), [900, 1200])

# 1. A decision stump: the best single split on one feature, chosen to minimise squared error.
def fit_stump(X, r):
    best = (np.inf, None)
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        for t in np.quantile(X[:, j], np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)):
            left = X[:, j] <= t
            pred = np.where(left, r[left].mean(), r[~left].mean())
            sse = ((r - pred) ** 2).sum()
            if sse < best[0]:
                best = (sse, (j, t, r[left].mean(), r[~left].mean()))
    return best[1]
stump_predict = lambda s, X: np.where(X[:, s[0]] <= s[1], s[2], s[3])

# 2. Gradient boosting: each new stump fits the residual errors of everything before it.
def boost(X, y, rounds, lr):
    base, stumps, pred = y.mean(), [], np.full(len(y), y.mean())
    for _ in range(rounds):
        s = fit_stump(X, y - pred)                  # residuals = negative gradient of squared error
        stumps.append(s)
        pred = pred + lr * stump_predict(s, X)
    return base, stumps
def boost_predict(model, X, lr):
    base, stumps = model
    return base + lr * sum(stump_predict(s, X) for s in stumps)
rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((a - b) ** 2)))

print(f"baseline (predict the mean): validation RMSE {rmse(y[va], np.full(len(va), y[tr].mean())):.3f}")
s = fit_stump(X[tr], y[tr])
print(f"one stump: split on feature {s[0]} at {s[1]:.2f}, validation RMSE {rmse(y[va], stump_predict(s, X[va])):.3f}")

# 3. Tuning: try settings on TRAIN, compare on VALIDATION, report the winner once on TEST.
results = []
for rounds in (10, 50, 200):
    for lr in (0.05, 0.3):
        m = boost(X[tr], y[tr], rounds, lr)
        results.append((rmse(y[va], boost_predict(m, X[va], lr)),
                        rmse(y[tr], boost_predict(m, X[tr], lr)), rounds, lr, m))
for v, t, r, lr, _ in sorted(results)[:3] + sorted(results)[-1:]:
    print(f"rounds={r:3d} lr={lr:<4}: train RMSE {t:.3f}  validation RMSE {v:.3f}")
best = min(results)
print(f"chosen rounds={best[2]}, lr={best[3]} -> test RMSE {rmse(y[te], boost_predict(best[4], X[te], best[3])):.3f}")

Output:

baseline (predict the mean): validation RMSE 1.272
one stump: split on feature 0 at 1.77, validation RMSE 0.655
rounds=200 lr=0.3 : train RMSE 0.636  validation RMSE 0.597
rounds= 50 lr=0.3 : train RMSE 0.639  validation RMSE 0.597
rounds=200 lr=0.05: train RMSE 0.641  validation RMSE 0.598
rounds= 10 lr=0.05: train RMSE 0.932  validation RMSE 0.939
chosen rounds=200, lr=0.3 -> test RMSE 0.661

What to notice:

  • One stump already halves the error, because flows jump when past return exceeds about 2%. That is exactly the split it found (feature 0 at 1.77).
  • Ten rounds at a small learning rate underfit (0.939). Many rounds or a larger rate reach about 0.60, close to the noise level of 0.6 built into the data, which is as good as any model can do.
  • Test RMSE (0.661) is a little worse than validation (0.597). Choosing the best of several settings on validation is slightly optimistic, which is why you report on an untouched test set.

5. Common mistakes

  1. No early stopping. Boosting keeps fitting noise.
  2. Tuning on the test set.
  3. Trusting gain importance for explanations. Use SHAP, and check stability.
  4. Ignoring monotonic constraints. In credit, risk should not fall as leverage rises. LightGBM and XGBoost support monotone constraints.
  5. Leaky features. Trees exploit leaks very efficiently (01).

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Extend the stump to a depth-2 tree and use it inside boosting. Compare validation RMSE.
  2. Add early stopping: stop boosting when validation RMSE hasn't improved for 20 rounds.
  3. Add subsampling (fit each stump on a random 70% of rows) and compare.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why are boosting residuals called gradients?
  2. What does a smaller learning rate trade off?
  3. Which tuning library does Databricks now recommend, and why?
  4. Why can test performance be worse than the best validation score?
  5. What is a monotonic constraint, and why use one in credit?

Answers

  1. For squared error, the residual is the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the prediction. Boosting follows gradients of whatever loss is used.
  2. More trees and training time, for better generalisation.
  3. Optuna for single-node tuning (Ray Tune for distributed tuning), because Hyperopt is no longer maintained.
  4. Picking the best of many settings on validation overfits to validation slightly.
  5. A rule that the prediction moves in one direction as a feature rises. It keeps the model consistent with economic sense and regulators' expectations.

8. Sources
